name: Tomas Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stockman and fix-it man at Redmoor, a beef farm with about a hundred and forty suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves, plus eighty hectares we cut for hay and silage. In November the cows come in to the big shed, so mornings are feeding, bedding with straw and checking for anyone coughing. Afternoons I'm usually under something, last week the baler, this week the gate on the cattle crush that keeps jamming.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned fixing things. Is that your background?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty years as a car mechanic at Hollins Motors on the ring road. Then the group that bought Hollins shut our branch, and they wanted young lads for the electric cars, not me. Gwen Askew, who owns Redmoor, knew me because I'd kept her old pickup alive for fifteen years. She said, you can fix anything, can you learn cows? Two years on, the honest answer is half yes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the half that's still no?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Reading the cattle. Gwen walks into the shed and says that heifer's going to calve tonight, and she's right, and I can't see it. I use an AI app every day, for the machinery mostly, I photograph a fault and talk it through, but I've also started asking it about calving signs. The pay's low and Mila, my wife, works at the pharmacy, so we're fine month to month but there's no fat on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a better spanner. I'd tell anyone that, I'm the one at the pub showing people how to ask it things. Hiring and pay carrying on as normal, nobody's going to complain about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be happy, maybe a bit disappointed. I like the stuff. I'd half hoped it would do more, like tell me which cow's going to calve from a photo, so I could catch up with Gwen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it more for the farm records, the cattle passports and the movement forms, which Gwen hates. I'd try to get her to pay me an extra few hours a week for doing the paperwork. And I'd keep tinkering, I'm building a little camera for the calving pen from bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit like a good tool turning up in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the camera in the calving pen.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's an old phone, a cheap solar panel and a box I made from a feed bucket. It streams the pen to my phone, so at two in the morning I can look from bed instead of walking out in the rain. Gwen called it nonsense, then asked me to put one in the other pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the app ever got something badly wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, on the baler. It told me with total confidence to replace a bearing, and it was a sheared pin, five minutes and a few pence. That's when I learned it's a clever apprentice, not a master. You still need your own hands on it.

S0.say: I'd say good, it's a better spanner, and I'd show people at the pub how to use it. Nobody will complain about hiring and pay carrying on.
S0.think: I'd be happy and maybe a bit disappointed, because I'd half hoped it could help me read the cows the way Gwen does.
S0.do: Uses AI to take on the cattle paperwork his boss hates and asks to be paid a few extra hours for it. Keeps building his home-made calving-pen camera.
S0.feel: Calm, like a good tool turning up in the post.
S0.quote: That's when I learned it's a clever apprentice, not a master.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is a natural tinkerer who sees AI as another tool in the box, with clear limits learned the hard way. He's honest that his weak spot is the cattle, not the machines. The home-made camera showed his habit of solving problems with whatever is lying around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, ten years gives everyone time to adjust. But I'd also say firms should keep taking apprentices, because that's how I learned, under an old mechanic called Frank, and that's not something a computer gives you. I'd say keep both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't scare me. I'll be retiring around when it's properly arrived. I'm more bothered that Redmoor will never take on a youngster after me, and Gwen is sixty-seven, so who's going to run this place?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd suggest to Gwen that we take a young person part-time, from the agricultural college, and that I teach them the machines while she teaches us both the cattle. I'd look up whether there's any grant for that. And I'd keep at my own learning, I'm doing an online course on cattle health in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, but with a question mark over the farm's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who was Frank, and why does he come to mind here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank was the old mechanic at Hollins when I was sixteen. He'd make me listen to an engine with a screwdriver against my ear, and he'd say the car's telling you, you just have to shut up. No app teaches you that. If firms stop taking beginners, nobody gets a Frank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Gwen go for a young part-timer, on a farm with thin margins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first. She'd say we can't afford it. I'd show her the numbers and maybe a grant, and say it's that or the farm dies with us. She's stubborn, but she listens to numbers.

S1.say: I'd say ten years gives everyone time to adjust, but firms should keep taking apprentices. Learning under an old hand isn't something a computer gives you.
S1.think: It doesn't scare me, since I'll be retiring as it arrives. I'm more bothered that Redmoor won't take a youngster after me, and the owner is sixty-seven.
S1.do: Proposes a part-time young worker from the agricultural college and looks for a grant to fund it. Keeps up an evening online course on cattle health.
S1.feel: Calm, with a question mark over the farm's future.
S1.quote: He'd say the car's telling you, you just have to shut up. No app teaches you that.
S1.fieldNote: His centre outlook came across as 'keep both' rather than taking sides. Even as a heavy AI user, he values learning beside an old hand, and Frank was a vivid memory. His worry was succession on the farm, not his own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tough on office people, and the politicians should agree on a sensible package rather than shout. Retraining that's actually useful, maybe some trades training, because we're short of mechanics and electricians. I'd say it on the farmers' forum where I post now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think about Mila. She's a pharmacy assistant, and a lot of her job is checking prescriptions on a screen and ordering stock, which sounds like exactly the routine stuff. Her wage is the steady half of ours. If it goes, we're in trouble fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Mila and look at what she could move into, maybe something where she's with people more, which the computers can't do as easily. I'd use the AI to find courses and costs for her. And I'd ask Gwen for the paperwork hours properly, in writing, as a bit of insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit guilty that I'm the one who loves these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I tell everyone at the pub how great it is, and here it is in your picture squeezing my own wife. I'd still use it. But I'd stop being quite so cheerful about it at the bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mila say about moving jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's fifty-six and she's not starting again, and I'd understand. Then she'd say, you started again at fifty-six, and I'd say, yes, and look how well I read cows. She'd laugh. She always gets me back.

S2.say: I'd say it's tough on office people and politicians should agree a sensible package, including trades training, since we're short of mechanics. I'd post it on the farmers' forum.
S2.think: I'd worry about Mila, whose pharmacy job is lots of screen checking and stock ordering. Her wage is the steady half of ours, and if it goes we're in trouble fast.
S2.do: Helps his wife look at moving into more people-facing work and uses AI to find courses and costs. Asks his boss to put the paperwork hours in writing as insurance.
S2.feel: Uneasy and a little guilty, since he's the one who loves these tools.
S2.quote: I'd still use it. But I'd stop being quite so cheerful about it at the bar.
S2.fieldNote: The office picture landed on his wife's pharmacy job, the steady part of their income. His honesty about feeling guilty as the family's AI fan was striking. Their back-and-forth about starting again showed warmth and humour under the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a fair settlement, some of the gains taxed and used to help people through, but not so heavy it kills the businesses that are doing well. Middle ground. I'd say that to both my brothers, who'd each think I was on the other one's side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be oddly well placed. Physical work's untouched, and I can fix things, which suddenly matters more when everyone else is losing desk jobs. Lots of people with money from shares might want hobby farms, and they'll need someone to keep their kit going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a little side line, weekends, fixing farm machinery and quad bikes for the new hobby farmers moving in. I'd use the AI to make a simple price list and a page online. I'd need a few hundred for tools, which I'd borrow from my brother rather than the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about Mila and the country, but if I'm honest, a bit excited about the side line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're on thin savings. Is borrowing from your brother wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's risky, I know. But my brother would let me pay it back slowly, and the bank wouldn't. If it didn't work, I'd sell the tools again. Tools always sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Pavel, who's a junior architect. You said skilled thinking work goes. He'd be the one ringing me. I'd tell him to come and learn to fix balers, half joking, and he'd say Dad, no, and then think about it.

S3.say: I'd say we need a fair settlement, taxing some gains to help people through but not killing businesses that do well. Middle ground, which annoys both my brothers.
S3.think: I'd be oddly well placed, since I can fix things and physical work is safe. New hobby farmers with share money will need someone to keep their kit going.
S3.do: Starts a weekend side line fixing machinery and quad bikes for new hobby farmers, with an AI-made price list and web page. Borrows a few hundred from his brother for tools rather than the bank.
S3.feel: Uneasy about his wife and the country, but a bit excited about the side line.
S3.quote: It's risky, I know. But my brother would let me pay it back slowly, and the bank wouldn't. If it didn't work, I'd sell the tools again. Tools always sell.
S3.fieldNote: He was the first person in this group to see the boom as a chance, through repairs for hobby farmers. His risk-taking was real but bounded by the knowledge that tools hold their value. His worry spread to his son, a junior architect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be phased, with real notice and money for retraining, and that whoever makes the robots should have to fund local repair training. I'd say it on the forum and probably write a letter to the paper, with the AI helping me sound less grumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in two minds. As a stockman I'm junior and I'm not good, so a robot that feeds and beds the cattle would do my morning better than me. But robots break, and someone has to fix them in a muddy yard at six in the morning. That could be me, if I move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gwen to let me be the one who chooses and sets up whatever robot comes, and I'd learn every bit of it. I'd do the manufacturer's training, even if I had to pay part of it. If Redmoor didn't want me, I'd go round the farms as a robot repair man, which I'd start building on weekends from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Proper anxious, because the money's so thin. But there's a part of me that's twenty again, looking at a new engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mila the night you decided to go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, either the robots take my job or I take the robots' job. She'd say, and what if neither happens and we're broke? And I wouldn't have a good answer, I'd just have the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You admitted the robot would do your mornings better than you. Was that hard to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it's true. I'm a mechanic who learned cows late. I'm not proud of the cow bit. I'm proud of the mechanic bit, and that's the bit the robots will need.

S4.say: I'd say it must be phased, with notice and retraining money, and robot makers should fund local repair training. I'd write to the paper with AI making me sound less grumpy.
S4.think: I'm in two minds. A robot would do my stockman mornings better than me, but robots break, and someone has to fix them in a muddy yard at six in the morning.
S4.do: Asks his boss to let him choose and set up the farm's robot and does the maker's training, paying part if needed. Starts a weekend robot repair round from day one in case the farm doesn't keep him.
S4.feel: Properly anxious because money is so thin, but part of him feels twenty again, looking at a new engine.
S4.quote: I'd say, love, either the robots take my job or I take the robots' job.
S4.fieldNote: He was clear-eyed that he's a weak stockman and a strong mechanic, and built his whole plan on the second. His wife's question about going broke had no good answer, and he admitted it. His mood was anxious rather than alarmed, held up by having a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because my money's so thin I can't afford to be wrong about the plan. What would help is cheap, local training on fixing these machines, open to people my age, and some help getting started on my own, a small loan with a fair rate. Give me the manuals and I'll learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Gwen. She's sixty-seven and owns the place, and none of these pictures say what happens to farmers like her. If she sells up to a big company, all my plans go out of the window.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's a good point. Anything else?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people should stop treating the AI like magic or like the devil. It's a clever apprentice. Treat it like one.

headlineQuote: I'd say, love, either the robots take my job or I take the robots' job.
portrait: Tomas Petrov is 58, a car mechanic for thirty years who became stockman and fix-it man on a 140-cow beef and hay farm two years ago after his garage branch closed. He uses an AI app every day, calls it a clever apprentice, and admits he still can't read cattle the way his 67-year-old boss Gwen can. He's calm in the early pictures, worried mainly about the farm's succession and his wife Mila's pharmacy job, and sees the boom as a chance for a weekend repair side line. In the robot picture he's anxious because money is thin, but he bets on being the person who fixes the robots.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because with so little money he can't afford his plan to fail.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap local training in fixing farm robots open to older workers, and a small fair loan to start his own repair work. He also worries what happens if his boss sells up.
